LightnerX ¶ LightnerX is a C++17 library for building applications that communicate using the INER semantic protocol. The CMake project provides the LightnerX target; it neither produces nor requires its own executable. The library provides types for representing messages, interpreters, callbacks, connection management, and a transport layer based on GameNetworkingSockets. Why LightnerX? ¶ LightnerX keeps client-server communication simple through a clear message model and modular components: Simple integration: connect networking and message handling through callbacks, while keeping control over initialization, update timing, and threads. Standardized communication: INER gives client and server a shared vocabulary for action requests, results, events, and informational updates, making each message's purpose and direction explicit. Modularity: compose message interpreters, connection management, and transport components according to your application's needs. Application flexibility: define your own message types and payloads while following the same communication model. INER defines the meaning of messages exchanged between an Authority and an Obedient. It does not define sockets, connections, or an execution model. These capabilities are provided by LightnerX's networking components and can be connected to the application according to the developer's needs. Build with CMake 3.22 or newer and a C++17 compiler. Public headers live under include/lightnerx/ . Byte views use tcb::span and results use zeus::expected . See Setup for dependencies and tested toolchains. Library, not a framework ¶ LightnerX provides reusable components. The consuming application decides: when to initialize and shut down components; how to run update() ; which threads to use; how to organize the connection lifecycle; which components to use or replace with its own implementations. For example, you can pass one complete INER message from your own transport to lightnerx::communication::MessageInterpreter . authorityInterpret does not require a connection. obedientInterpret requires a lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager registration: add() accepts only live GNS handles, so arbitrary identifiers from another transport are not supported by that path. The manager stores its own mapping and does not use GNS connection userdata. Key concepts ¶ Authority: controls internal states and receives intentions from the Obedient. Obedient: sends intentions to the Authority and receives events and responses. Event: an occurrence communicated by the Authority. Response: the result of an intention sent by the Obedient. Intention: an action request sent to the Authority. Notification: information sent to the Authority without requesting a state change. INER message flow ¶ The INER protocol defines four message types exchanged between the Authority and the Obedient: Choose the message type according to its purpose and direction. In a typical client-server application, the server acts as the Authority and the client as the Obedient. Message type Direction When to use it Examples Intention Client → Server Request an action that the Authority must evaluate. Move a player, fire a weapon, use an item, join a match. Notification Client → Server Report information without requesting a change to the Authority's internal state. Report measured ping/latency, FPS, or client diagnostics. Event Server → Client Communicate an occurrence or state update from the Authority. A player joined, an entity moved, a projectile spawned, a match started. Response Server → Client Return the outcome of a specific Intention, linked by its correlationId . Movement approved, firing denied because ammunition is insufficient, an action partially applied, or processing failed. These examples describe application-defined messages; LightnerX does not provide built-in gameplay commands or telemetry formats. A Response reports an Intention's outcome, while an Event communicates an occurrence to the relevant clients. flowchart LR A["🖥️ AUTHORITY

When sending, lightnerx::network::Target lets you select a connection, a group, or a broadcast with or without exceptions. Create the components ¶ The manager maps handles to internal client IDs. Register ID 47 so that the interpreter recognizes notifications sent by the client in this example. using namespace std::chrono_literals; namespace network = lightnerx::network; namespace communication = lightnerx::communication; network::Server server; network::ConnectionManager connections{30, 30}; communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; communication::NotificationRegistry notifications; notifications.registerId(47); Track connections ¶ The callbacks keep the manager up to date. If registering a connection fails, the server requests its disconnection. server.addClientConnectedCallback([&](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (!connections.add(connection)) { if (const auto result = server.disconnectConnection(connection, false); !result) { std::cout << "Failed to disconnect: " << result.error().message() << ' '; } } }); server.addClientDisconnectedCallback([&](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (const auto id = connections.getClientId(connection)) { connections.remove(*id); } }); Receive messages ¶ Forward the received bytes to obedientInterpret . The interpreter's callback delivers the message and the internal client ID. In this example, the payload is text and is read during the callback. server.addClientReceivedMessageCallback( [&](tcb::span bytes, HSteamNetConnection connection) { interpreter.obedientInterpret(bytes, notifications, connection, connections); } ); interpreter.addObedientInterpretedMessageCallback( [](communication::Message message, std::uint16_t clientId) { const auto text = message.payload.empty() ? std::string_view{} : std::string_view{ reinterpret_cast(message.payload.data()), message.payload.size() }; std::cout << "Client " << clientId << ": " << text << ' '; } ); Start the server ¶ Start listening on port 41333 , with an established connection timeout of 3000 ms, and reserve one slot for the batcher's pending message. if (const auto result = server.start(41333, 3000); !result) { std::cout << "Failed to start: " << result.error().message() << ' '; return 1; } network::initMessagesBatcher(1); Prepare an event ¶ Convert the text to bytes and include the header and payload in the total size. For Event , the size is shifted one bit to the left. Type 990 is chosen by the application. const std::string_view greeting = "Hello, World!"; const auto payload = tcb::as_bytes(tcb::span{greeting}); const communication::Event event{ // The least significant bit distinguishes Event from Response. static_cast((sizeof(communication::Event) + payload.size()) << 1), 990 }; Update and send ¶ update() processes the network. The converter creates an OutboundMessage , which is passed directly to queueMessage . Target::broadcast() selects the connections registered at flush time. while (true) { if (const auto result = server.update(); !result) { std::cout << "Failed to update: " << result.error().message() << ' '; break; } if (const auto result = network::queueMessage(communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, network::Target::broadcast())); !result) { std::cout << "Failed to queue: " << result.error().message() << ' '; break; } if (const auto result = network::flushAll(connections); !result) { std::cout << "Failed to send: " << result.error().message() << ' '; break; } std::this_thread::sleep_for(3s); } queueMessage takes ownership of the message, including when it returns an error; the application does not call Release() afterward. flushAll processes the queue and releases the messages. The three-second interval is a choice made for this example; the application defines its own update rate. Shut down the server ¶ After exiting the loop due to an error, close the server. Returning 1 signals an exit due to failure in this example. server.close(); return 1; Client example ¶ The client connects to the server at 127.0.0.1:41333 , prints the received events, and sends a notification with the same text. Run the server and client in separate processes. Create the components ¶ The empty manager satisfies the flushAll signature. Sending to the server individually uses the client's connection handle directly. using namespace std::chrono_literals; namespace network = lightnerx::network; namespace communication = lightnerx::communication; network::Client client; network::ConnectionManager connections{0, 0}; // Required by flush, without broadcast. communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; Receive messages from the server ¶ Forward the bytes to authorityInterpret , which interprets messages from the Authority. The callback below prints the text payload agreed upon by these examples and handles empty payloads. client.addServerReceivedMessageCallback([&](tcb::span bytes) { interpreter.authorityInterpret(bytes); }); interpreter.addAuthorityInterpretedMessageCallback([](communication::Message message) { const auto text = message.payload.empty() ? std::string_view{} : std::string_view{ reinterpret_cast(message.payload.data()), message.payload.size() }; std::cout << "Server: " << text << ' '; }); The callbacks use the bytes during the call. To retain a received payload, copy its bytes into application storage before returning. Start and connect ¶ Initialize the client, request a connection to the server, and reserve space in the batcher. The connection will be tracked during calls to update() . if (const auto result = client.start(); !result) { std::cout << "Failed to start: " << result.error().message() << ' '; return 1; } if (const auto result = client.connect("127.0.0.1", 41333); !result) { std::cout << "Failed to connect: " << result.error().message() << ' '; return 1; } network::initMessagesBatcher(1); Prepare a notification ¶ Notification uses the total size directly, without bit shifting. ID 47 corresponds to the registration made on the server. const std::string_view greeting = "Hello, World!"; const auto payload = tcb::as_bytes(tcb::span{greeting}); const communication::Notification notification{ static_cast(sizeof(communication::Notification) + payload.size()), 47 // The server must register this ID in NotificationRegistry. }; Update and send to the server ¶ Process up to 32 messages per update and send when isConnected() indicates an established connection. Target::single selects the server's handle. while (true) { if (const auto result = client.update(32); !result) { std::cout << "Failed to update: " << result.error().message() << ' '; break; } if (client.isConnected()) { if (const auto result = network::queueMessage(communication::notification2OutboundMessage( notification, payload, network::Target::single(client.getServerHConn()))); !result) { std::cout << "Failed to queue: " << result.error().message() << ' '; break; } if (const auto result = network::flushAll(connections); !result) { std::cout << "Failed to send: " << result.error().message() << ' '; break; } } std::this_thread::sleep_for(3000ms); } Shut down the client ¶ When exiting due to an error, the Client destructor closes the connection and shuts down the network. Returning 1 indicates the failure that interrupted the example. return 1; // The Client destructor closes the connection and shuts down the network. docs.text: One started Client or Server owns networking when the process uses a single LightnerX library instance. Applications with multiple plugins should link them to the same shared LightnerX library. Both classes have stable addresses and cannot be copied or moved. Server::close() and either owner's destructor release the runtime; a client can disconnect and reconnect without being destroyed. Direct networkInit() / networkKill() remain available when using the transport without a wrapper. See API reference for shutdown, callback exceptions, reentrancy and message validation contracts.

This reception behavior is more permissive than the recommended emission formats. If the total size matches the supplied span and the header is complete, additional bytes in approved and failure responses are accepted but ignored; additional bytes in denied responses are delivered. The returned object contains the message pointer and the destination target . Allocation failure throws std::bad_alloc ; a byte count that cannot fit the GNS allocation API throws std::length_error . No message ownership is transferred on these exceptions. Initialize the network before using them. The caller fills in the size field according to the binary representation and passes the created object to queueMessage , which takes ownership of it. If the object is never passed to the queue, the caller must release it with Release() . For the recommended emission formats, provide {} as the payload for approved, denied, or failure responses; for partial approval, provide the bytes defined by the application. Converters copy the supplied payload without enforcing these status-specific recommendations. <lightnerx/network/network_manager.hpp> ¶ Functions for controlling the global network state: bool networkInit(); void networkKill(); bool isNetworkInitialized(); networkInit() initializes GameNetworkingSockets and is idempotent. isNetworkInitialized() reports whether the registered runtime and interface exist. Without a started wrapper, networkKill() releases queued messages, shuts down networking and resets the state; it is safe to call repeatedly and initialize again. A single LightnerX library instance allows exactly one started Client or Server to own the runtime. Starting the same owner again returns operation_in_progress . Starting another owner returns device_or_resource_busy . Both types are noncopyable and nonmovable. A failed start releases resources created by that attempt and permits retry. If the application initialized the network manually, the failed attempt preserves the runtime, existing connections and pending messages. A successful start adopts that runtime. The server close or the client destructor releases ownership and shuts down the adopted runtime. For multiple plugins, use one shared LightnerX library across the process. While a wrapper owns the runtime, networkKill() defers shutdown until that owner releases it. The interface remains usable and isNetworkInitialized() remains true in the meantime. Direct external GameNetworkingSockets_Kill() and raw RunCallbacks() during wrapper ownership are unsupported; use LightnerX lifecycle and update operations. Synchronize all network operations across threads in the application. g_bNetworkInitialized is a legacy public flag maintained by LightnerX. Callbacks ¶ void addClientConnectedCallback( std::function<void(HSteamNetConnection)> callback ); void addClientDisconnectedCallback( std::function<void(HSteamNetConnection)> callback ); void addClientReceivedMessageCallback( std::function<void( tcb::span<const std::byte>, HSteamNetConnection )> callback ); Lifecycle ¶ zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> start( int port, std::uint32_t timeoutConnected ); zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> update(); zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> disconnectConnection( HSteamNetConnection hConn, bool enableLinger ); void close() noexcept; start() initializes the network and opens the listen socket on the specified port (1–65535); timeoutConnected is passed to GameNetworkingSockets in milliseconds. Its maximum accepted value is INT32_MAX (2,147,483,647 ms), although the parameter type is uint32_t . For an unstarted server, a value above this limit returns std::errc::invalid_argument before initializing the network or opening the listen socket. Calling start() on an already started server returns operation_in_progress first. After a successful start, update() processes network callbacks and up to one available message in the poll group. The connection callback runs after acceptance and assignment to the poll group. If a callback disconnects that client, disconnection callbacks run as part of the disconnect call and subsequent connection callbacks for that handle are skipped. The receive callback provides the bytes and the source handle. The bytes remain valid during these callbacks. disconnectConnection() requests that a specific connection be closed and, on success, calls the disconnection callbacks. enableLinger is forwarded to the transport to control the attempt to send pending data when closing. close() closes the listen socket, destroys the poll group, and shuts down GameNetworkingSockets. It is idempotent and also runs from the destructor. A close requested inside a callback is completed after the outer operation releases received messages; remaining callbacks in that dispatch are skipped. Bulk close does not emit individual disconnection callbacks: clear application registrations before reusing a manager for a new session. Disconnection callbacks receive a historical handle after closure; ConnectionManager::getClientId() remains valid until remove() . <lightnerx/network/client.hpp> ¶ lightnerx::network::Client ¶ Client that connects to an IP address and processes messages from the connection to the server. void addServerReceivedMessageCallback( const std::function<void(tcb::span<const std::byte>)>& callback ); zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> start(); zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> connect( std::string_view ip, int port ); zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> update( int maxMessagesToProcess ); zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> disconnect( bool enableLinger ); bool isConnected() const noexcept; HSteamNetConnection getServerHConn() const noexcept; start() initializes the transport. connect() initiates the connection to a numeric IPv4 or IPv6 literal and the separate port argument. IPv6 may be enclosed in brackets. Hostnames, scope identifiers, embedded ports, embedded NULs and trailing characters are rejected with invalid_argument . After calling connect() , monitor isConnected() while calling update() to observe the connection being established. update() runs network callbacks and processes up to the specified number of messages; values less than or equal to zero run only the network callbacks. getServerHConn() returns the handle used to send messages to the server, for example with Target::single(client.getServerHConn()) . The receive callback is stored by the client, and the provided span remains valid during its execution. disconnect() requests that the connection be closed and forwards enableLinger to the transport. On success it immediately invalidates the handle and clears isConnected() , allowing another connect() on the same instance. It retains ownership of the runtime until the destructor. Disconnecting inside a receive callback stops further callbacks and messages from that receive batch; all acquired messages are released. The destructor closes the existing connection and shuts down networking. <lightnerx/network/connection_manager.hpp> ¶ lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager ¶ Maintains the mapping between internal IDs and connection handles. ConnectionManager(int initialReserve, int maxCapacity); HSteamNetConnection getHSteamNetConnection( std::uint16_t id ) const noexcept; std::optional<std::uint16_t> getClientId( HSteamNetConnection hConn ) const noexcept; std::optional<std::uint16_t> add(HSteamNetConnection hConn); void remove(int id); int getOnlineCount() const noexcept; template<class Callback> void forEach(const Callback& callback) const; initialReserve reserves storage space, and maxCapacity defines the maximum number of registered connections. add registers a handle and returns the assigned ID, or an empty std::optional when registration is not performed. remove unregisters the ID; closing the connection is handled by the networking component. Copying a manager produces independent registrations. If copy assignment throws, the destination preserves its mappings, count, capacity and ID allocation state. A successful move transfers the registrations and ID allocation state. The source becomes empty, retains its configured maximum capacity and starts assigning IDs at 1 again. getHSteamNetConnection looks up a handle by its internal ID and returns 0 when there is no handle at that position. getClientId looks up the ID in this manager's local registration map, independently of GNS userdata or whether the handle has since closed. getOnlineCount returns the number of active registrations. forEach calls the callback for each active registration, providing the ID and handle: connections.forEach( [](std::uint16_t id, HSteamNetConnection connection) { // Send to or inspect the connection. } ); <lightnerx/network/transport.hpp> ¶ Direct sending ¶ zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> sendToConnection( tcb::span<const std::byte> message, HSteamNetConnection hConn ); Forwards the bytes to GameNetworkingSockets with the reliable send option. After checking the network and connection handle, the function returns std::errc::message_size if the byte count exceeds the transport's 32-bit length field. The return value indicates whether the transport accepted the send. This function uses the transport directly, bypassing the batcher queue. Sending to a group ¶ zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> sendToConnections( tcb::span<const std::byte> message, const std::vector<HSteamNetConnection> connections ); Forwards the same bytes to each handle in the vector. Attempts all destinations and returns the first error encountered, if any. Broadcast ¶ zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> broadcast( tcb::span<const std::byte> message, const lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager& connectionManager, const std::vector<HSteamNetConnection> exceptions ); Forwards the same bytes to the connections registered in ConnectionManager , except for the handles in exceptions . Attempts all selected destinations and returns the first error encountered, if any. For direct sending, the third argument is required; use {} to include all connections: const auto all = lightnerx::network::broadcast(bytes, connections, {}); const auto others = lightnerx::network::broadcast(bytes, connections, {connectionToSkip}); The examples above are independent calls; check the result of each send used by the application. To defer sending until a flush, use Target::broadcast with queueMessage . <lightnerx/network/target.hpp> ¶ lightnerx::network::Target ¶ Represents the destination of a queued message. Use the static factories to create the destination: static Target single(HSteamNetConnection conn); static Target group(std::vector<HSteamNetConnection> connections); static Target broadcast( std::vector<HSteamNetConnection> exceptions = {} ); [[nodiscard]] bool isBroadcast() const noexcept; [[nodiscard]] bool isSingle() const noexcept; [[nodiscard]] bool isGroup() const noexcept; single selects one connection. group stores the provided vector of handles. broadcast() selects all connections registered in the ConnectionManager used during the flush. broadcast({handle}) excludes the specified handle; the vector can contain multiple exceptions. The factories only describe destinations. isSingle() , isGroup() and isBroadcast() report which destination is stored. Broadcast queries connections at flush time, while a group uses the list stored in Target . Public fields: std::variant< std::monostate, std::vector<HSteamNetConnection>, HSteamNetConnection > connection; std::vector<HSteamNetConnection> broadcastExceptions; <lightnerx/network/message_batch.hpp> ¶ lightnerx::network::OutboundMessage ¶ struct OutboundMessage { SteamNetworkingMessage_t* message; Target target; }; Batcher ¶ void initMessagesBatcher(int capacity); void clearMessagesBatcher() noexcept; zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> queueMessage(OutboundMessage message); zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> flushAll( const ConnectionManager& connectionManager ); initMessagesBatcher reserves space in the batcher's shared queue. Call it before queuing with the number of messages you want to be able to keep pending. The first access constructs the queue, including when a consumer reserves capacity before main() . Reserving preserves pending messages. A negative capacity throws std::invalid_argument . queueMessage receives an OutboundMessage by value and moves it into the queue. The message allocated by the converter is retained, without allocating another message or copying the bytes. If the reserved capacity is occupied, it releases the received message and returns std::errc::not_enough_memory . If message.message is null, it returns std::errc::invalid_argument without queuing. flushAll processes each message separately by sending it to an individual connection, a group, or a broadcast. ConnectionManager is a required argument and provides the broadcast recipients. The function releases all internal messages and empties the queue even when errors occur, returning the last error among the send operations. An empty queue returns success. Calling queueMessage consumes the message, both on success and on error. Pass an existing object with std::move(outbound) or use a converter's result directly. Afterward, do not access, release, or requeue the message. OutboundMessage contains a raw pointer: std::move allows the destination to be moved, but does not automatically set the pointer to null in the original object. Copying the object does not duplicate the message either; therefore, do not pass copies of the same message to the queue. If you never pass a created message to the queue, release it exactly once with Release() . With the network and batcher initialized, and event , payload , connection , and connections defined by the application, typical usage after a converter is: auto outbound = lightnerx::communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, lightnerx::network::Target::single(connection) ); const auto queued = lightnerx::network::queueMessage(std::move(outbound)); if (!queued) { std::cout << "Failed to queue: " << queued.error().message() << '\n'; } else if (const auto flushed = lightnerx::network::flushAll(connections); !flushed) { std::cout << "Failed to send: " << flushed.error().message() << '\n'; } You can also queue multiple messages before calling flushAll . The batcher keeps each message separate, and the application chooses when to flush. Validation and callback behavior ¶ Both interpretation methods accept exactly one complete message. The declared total size must equal the supplied span and include the entire header. Authority sizes are decoded from 15 bits (maximum 32767 bytes); Obedient sizes use 16 bits (maximum 65535 bytes). Truncated headers, mismatched sizes, unknown response status and unregistered Obedient origins produce no callback, matching the existing void parser interface. There is no incremental or concatenated-message framing. Callbacks run synchronously. Registration during a callback is safe; newly registered callbacks participate from the next dispatch, including a nested interpretation. Existing callback objects retain mutable state. Receive/interpreter/ forEach exceptions propagate to their caller, with received buffers released even when a client batch is interrupted. Exceptions from GNS status callbacks are caught at the boundary and the first exception is rethrown by Server::update() after RunCallbacks() returns. A throwing callback ends its current callback sequence. Recursive update() returns operation_in_progress . Callbacks may disconnect or request Server::close() ; do not destroy or assign the component executing a callback. Referenced objects must remain alive until dispatch finishes. A negative receive result returns io_error , distinct from an empty queue; the client also clears and closes its failed connection. Updating an unstarted/closed wrapper returns not_connected . ConnectionManager owns an independent, bidirectional mapping; it neither reads nor writes GNS userdata. A handle may be registered once per manager. Adding a duplicate, invalid handle, or a handle beyond capacity returns nullopt . Different managers may independently register the same valid handle. getClientId() returns nullopt for an absent registration, including handle zero, and retains a registered identity after transport closure until removal. IDs range from 1 to 65535 and are recycled; negative capacities throw invalid_argument , capacity above 65535 is capped. forEach visits the index range present on entry, safely allowing add/remove; it may observe replacements within that range but does not extend traversal for vector growth. The batch queue is global. initMessagesBatcher() reserves capacity without discarding queued messages. clearMessagesBatcher() releases pending messages and preserves capacity; actual network shutdown and queue destruction also release pending messages. flushAll() releases every queued message if a send throws, then propagates the exception; with returned error codes it attempts all entries and returns the last error. Serialize all batch operations, including clearing and shutdown.

docs.text: Functions for controlling the global network state: bool networkInit(); void networkKill(); bool isNetworkInitialized(); networkInit() initializes GameNetworkingSockets and is idempotent. isNetworkInitialized() reports whether the registered runtime and interface exist. Without a started wrapper, networkKill() releases queued messages, shuts down networking and resets the state; it is safe to call repeatedly and initialize again. A single LightnerX library instance allows exactly one started Client or Server to own the runtime. Starting the same owner again returns operation_in_progress . Starting another owner returns device_or_resource_busy . Both types are noncopyable and nonmovable. A failed start releases resources created by that attempt and permits retry. If the application initialized the network manually, the failed attempt preserves the runtime, existing connections and pending messages. A successful start adopts that runtime. The server close or the client destructor releases ownership and shuts down the adopted runtime. For multiple plugins, use one shared LightnerX library across the process. While a wrapper owns the runtime, networkKill() defers shutdown until that owner releases it. The interface remains usable and isNetworkInitialized() remains true in the meantime. Direct external GameNetworkingSockets_Kill() and raw RunCallbacks() during wrapper ownership are unsupported; use LightnerX lifecycle and update operations. Synchronize all network operations across threads in the application. g_bNetworkInitialized is a legacy public flag maintained by LightnerX. Use isNetworkInitialized() to query the runtime state and the lifecycle functions to change it. k_invalidConnection is declared once in <lightnerx/network/network_manager.hpp> , which is included by the client and transport headers.

docs.text: void initMessagesBatcher(int capacity); void clearMessagesBatcher() noexcept; zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> queueMessage(OutboundMessage message); zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> flushAll( const ConnectionManager& connectionManager ); initMessagesBatcher reserves space in the batcher's shared queue. Call it before queuing with the number of messages you want to be able to keep pending. The first access constructs the queue, including when a consumer reserves capacity before main() . Reserving preserves pending messages. A negative capacity throws std::invalid_argument . queueMessage receives an OutboundMessage by value and moves it into the queue. The message allocated by the converter is retained, without allocating another message or copying the bytes. If the reserved capacity is occupied, it releases the received message and returns std::errc::not_enough_memory . If message.message is null, it returns std::errc::invalid_argument without queuing. flushAll processes each message separately by sending it to an individual connection, a group, or a broadcast. ConnectionManager is a required argument and provides the broadcast recipients. The function releases all internal messages and empties the queue even when errors occur, returning the last error among the send operations. An empty queue returns success. Calling queueMessage consumes the message, both on success and on error. Pass an existing object with std::move(outbound) or use a converter's result directly. Afterward, do not access, release, or requeue the message. OutboundMessage contains a raw pointer: std::move allows the destination to be moved, but does not automatically set the pointer to null in the original object. Copying the object does not duplicate the message either; therefore, do not pass copies of the same message to the queue. If you never pass a created message to the queue, release it exactly once with Release() . With the network and batcher initialized, and event , payload , connection , and connections defined by the application, typical usage after a converter is: auto outbound = lightnerx::communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, lightnerx::network::Target::single(connection) ); const auto queued = lightnerx::network::queueMessage(std::move(outbound)); if (!queued) { std::cout << "Failed to queue: " << queued.error().message() << '\n'; } else if (const auto flushed = lightnerx::network::flushAll(connections); !flushed) { std::cout << "Failed to send: " << flushed.error().message() << '\n'; } You can also queue multiple messages before calling flushAll . The batcher keeps each message separate, and the application chooses when to flush.

docs.text: Both interpretation methods accept exactly one complete message. The declared total size must equal the supplied span and include the entire header. Authority sizes are decoded from 15 bits (maximum 32767 bytes); Obedient sizes use 16 bits (maximum 65535 bytes). Truncated headers, mismatched sizes, unknown response status and unregistered Obedient origins produce no callback, matching the existing void parser interface. There is no incremental or concatenated-message framing. Callbacks run synchronously. Registration during a callback is safe; newly registered callbacks participate from the next dispatch, including a nested interpretation. Existing callback objects retain mutable state. Receive/interpreter/ forEach exceptions propagate to their caller, with received buffers released even when a client batch is interrupted. Exceptions from GNS status callbacks are caught at the boundary and the first exception is rethrown by Server::update() after RunCallbacks() returns. A throwing callback ends its current callback sequence. Recursive update() returns operation_in_progress . Callbacks may disconnect or request Server::close() ; do not destroy or assign the component executing a callback. Referenced objects must remain alive until dispatch finishes. A negative receive result returns io_error , distinct from an empty queue; the client also clears and closes its failed connection. Updating an unstarted/closed wrapper returns not_connected . ConnectionManager owns an independent, bidirectional mapping; it neither reads nor writes GNS userdata. A handle may be registered once per manager. Adding a duplicate, invalid handle, or a handle beyond capacity returns nullopt . Different managers may independently register the same valid handle. getClientId() returns nullopt for an absent registration, including handle zero, and retains a registered identity after transport closure until removal. IDs range from 1 to 65535 and are recycled; negative capacities throw invalid_argument , capacity above 65535 is capped. forEach visits the index range present on entry, safely allowing add/remove; it may observe replacements within that range but does not extend traversal for vector growth. The batch queue is global. initMessagesBatcher() reserves capacity without discarding queued messages. clearMessagesBatcher() releases pending messages and preserves capacity; actual network shutdown and queue destruction also release pending messages. flushAll() releases every queued message if a send throws, then propagates the exception; with returned error codes it attempts all entries and returns the last error. Serialize all batch operations, including clearing and shutdown.

docs.text: Correções da auditoria LightnerX — registro histórico ¶ Este documento preserva os resultados da auditoria de 12/11/2026, anterior à migração. O LightnerX atual usa C++17 e headers clássicos; a validação atual está em Migração C++17 e as instruções de build em Setup . Os caminhos da tabela abaixo foram atualizados para os arquivos atuais; os headers correspondentes estão em include/lightnerx/ . Números, logs e limitações descritos como históricos referem-se exclusivamente à auditoria. Revisão de origem: 8e5a352 . Dependência GNS: d534c19 . Auditoria lida: LightnerX-audit.md . Naquela auditoria, C++26, módulos, GameNetworkingSockets, representação binária INER e queueMessage(OutboundMessage) com Target foram preservados. Evidências e testes históricos ¶ A suíte normal passou nos oito testes, sem testes ignorados. Resultados locais: build/audit/test-results.xml e build/audit/Testing/Temporary/LastTest.log . A execução instrumentada final também passou nos oito testes, sem testes ignorados e sem diagnósticos dos sanitizadores habilitados (53,47 segundos). Resultados: build/audit-sanitizers/test-results.xml e build/audit-sanitizers/Testing/Temporary/LastTest.log . A suíte normal levou 131,90 segundos, incluindo a compilação do consumidor. Os limites abaixo são parte da validação, não uma garantia de ausência de todos os defeitos possíveis. A classificação final é de 13 itens corrigidos e validados e LX-14 corrigido, mas parcialmente validado pelas restrições de instrumentação explicitadas. Os executáveis connection_manager , messages e lifecycle importam os módulos reais e usam GNS real. Há testes de reinicialização, estados inválidos, identidade, serialização, ownership e callbacks. integration executa Client e Server em processos separados sobre UDP local. Testa três sessões, mensagens, reconexão, desconexão iniciada pelos dois lados, identidade após fechamento, exceção de admissão, registro reentrante de callbacks, update recursivo e encerramento/reinicialização do servidor. consumer configura um projeto pai independente, inclui headers Steam e importa módulos ligando somente o target LightnerX . Os três testes Python suplementares compilam corpos de produção sem as declarações de módulos. Interfaces controladas permitem esgotar os 65.535 IDs, devolver alocação nula e provocar erros de recebimento/liberação. Eles não substituem os testes dos módulos reais. Contadores verificam a liberação de mensagens, inclusive após uma parte do lote já ter sido processada. Reproduções anteriores às correções incluíram: Client copiável; três mensagens retidas após exceção; desconexão com connected=true ; erro de recebimento reportado como sucesso; inicialização global verdadeira com interface nula; start simultâneo/repetido aceito; optional inválido com valor zero; duplicatas; overflow de IDs; tamanho INER inválido entregue; alocação nula causando falha. O consumidor original não encontrava o header Steam e compilava em C++17. O teste de domínio também foi aplicado ao arquivo original de 8e5a352 e falhou em exhausted ID domain must reject add ( build/audit/id-baseline.log ). Reprodução com a versão C++17 atual ¶ Os comandos abaixo executam a suíte atual; não recriam os oito testes históricos. Para reproduzir o ambiente antigo, use a revisão e a toolchain daquela auditoria. O problema UBSan/módulos descrito abaixo não se aplica mais à implementação C++17; somente a incompatibilidade de vptr com GNS sem RTTI permanece. cmake -S . -B build/audit -G Ninja \ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DLIGHTNERX_BUILD_TESTS=ON cmake --build build/audit --parallel 2 ctest --test-dir build/audit --output-on-failure --output-junit test-results.xml -j 2 cmake -S . -B build/audit-sanitizers -G Ninja \ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DLIGHTNERX_BUILD_TESTS=ON \ -DLIGHTNERX_SANITIZERS=address,undefined cmake --build build/audit-sanitizers --parallel 2 ctest --test-dir build/audit-sanitizers --output-on-failure --output-junit test-results.xml -j 2 O teste UDP e LeakSanitizer precisam de permissões que o sandbox inicial não oferecia. A execução final usa o ambiente autorizado fora dessa restrição. O limite dos testes que compilam código foi ampliado para 180 segundos após um timeout de compilação concorrente; os limites de runtime permanecem delimitados. Limites históricos dos sanitizadores ¶ Os módulos LightnerX e os consumidores foram compilados com ASan. Os três testes suplementares usam ASan e UBSan, com -fno-sanitize-recover=all , para que qualquer diagnóstico habilitado resulte em falha. A biblioteca padrão e o GNS não foram instrumentados nem tiveram seus fontes alterados. GCC 15.2 aborta com erro interno cp/module.cc:10037 ao compilar estes módulos com UBSan. Isso foi reproduzido tanto instrumentando std quanto deixando std sem instrumentação; portanto não se declara cobertura UBSan dos módulos reais. O GNS vendorizado usa -fno-rtti . Uma reprodução independente, contendo apenas Init/CreatePollGroup/DestroyPollGroup/Kill de GNS, já produz o diagnóstico vptr do UBSan, sem usar LightnerX. O mesmo programa passa quando somente essa checagem é desabilitada ( build/audit/gns-ubsan-probe.cpp e .log ). Por isso apenas o teste suplementar de ciclo de vida, que chama a biblioteca real, usa -fno-sanitize=vptr . Os outros dois testes suplementares não precisam dessa exclusão. Esse diagnóstico foi investigado mesmo quando CTest inicialmente reportou sucesso por causa do modo recuperável padrão do UBSan. API pública e contratos preservados ¶ Client e Server não podem mais ser copiados ou movidos. Server ganha destrutor com limpeza automática; close() é idempotente e noexcept . Apenas um Client ou Server iniciado possui a rede por processo. Start repetido retorna operation_in_progress ; outro owner retorna device_or_resource_busy . networkKill() não invalida um wrapper ativo; o encerramento ocorre quando o owner libera os recursos. Raw GNS Kill/RunCallbacks durante esse ownership não são operações suportadas. disconnect() limpa o estado local imediatamente. Erros de recebimento passam a retornar io_error . Callbacks podem lançar; buffers são liberados e a exceção é propagada. Não se deve destruir o objeto que está despachando um callback. forEach deixa de ser incondicionalmente noexcept . getClientId() consulta pertencimento ao manager e não userdata GNS. A identidade persiste até remoção explícita. O manager deixa userdata para a aplicação. Capacidades negativas são rejeitadas; o domínio é limitado a 65535. Conversores mantêm assinaturas e lançam bad_alloc / length_error em falhas. Mensagens recebidas com tamanho inconsistente são rejeitadas sem callback, conforme a interface de parsing existente, que retorna void . Adicionados clearMessagesBatcher() e Target::isGroup() . A API queueMessage() /Target permanece; mensagens pendentes são liberadas no encerramento e após exceções. initMessagesBatcher() não descarta a fila. Há uma única constante pública k_invalidConnection . CMake agora propaga C++17 e os requisitos públicos GNS. O consumidor inclui os headers clássicos descritos em Setup . Não há decisão arquitetural pendente para as correções adotadas. As restrições de múltiplas instâncias, transporte próprio, callbacks e framing foram explicitadas de forma conservadora. docs.text: Os módulos LightnerX e os consumidores foram compilados com ASan. Os três testes suplementares usam ASan e UBSan, com -fno-sanitize-recover=all , para que qualquer diagnóstico habilitado resulte em falha. A biblioteca padrão e o GNS não foram instrumentados nem tiveram seus fontes alterados. GCC 15.2 aborta com erro interno cp/module.cc:10037 ao compilar estes módulos com UBSan. Isso foi reproduzido tanto instrumentando std quanto deixando std sem instrumentação; portanto não se declara cobertura UBSan dos módulos reais. O GNS vendorizado usa -fno-rtti . Uma reprodução independente, contendo apenas Init/CreatePollGroup/DestroyPollGroup/Kill de GNS, já produz o diagnóstico vptr do UBSan, sem usar LightnerX. O mesmo programa passa quando somente essa checagem é desabilitada ( build/audit/gns-ubsan-probe.cpp e .log ). docs.text: Client e Server não podem mais ser copiados ou movidos. Server ganha destrutor com limpeza automática; close() é idempotente e noexcept . Apenas um Client ou Server iniciado possui a rede por processo. Start repetido retorna operation_in_progress ; outro owner retorna device_or_resource_busy . networkKill() não invalida um wrapper ativo; o encerramento ocorre quando o owner libera os recursos. Raw GNS Kill/RunCallbacks durante esse ownership não são operações suportadas. disconnect() limpa o estado local imediatamente. Erros de recebimento passam a retornar io_error . Callbacks podem lançar; buffers são liberados e a exceção é propagada. Não se deve destruir o objeto que está despachando um callback. forEach deixa de ser incondicionalmente noexcept . getClientId() consulta pertencimento ao manager e não userdata GNS. A identidade persiste até remoção explícita. O manager deixa userdata para a aplicação. Capacidades negativas são rejeitadas; o domínio é limitado a 65535. Conversores mantêm assinaturas e lançam bad_alloc / length_error em falhas. Mensagens recebidas com tamanho inconsistente são rejeitadas sem callback, conforme a interface de parsing existente, que retorna void . Adicionados clearMessagesBatcher() e Target::isGroup() . A API queueMessage() /Target permanece; mensagens pendentes são liberadas no encerramento e após exceções. initMessagesBatcher() não descarta a fila. Há uma única constante pública k_invalidConnection . CMake agora propaga C++17 e os requisitos públicos GNS. O consumidor inclui os headers clássicos descritos em Setup . Não há decisão arquitetural pendente para as correções adotadas. As restrições de múltiplas instâncias, transporte próprio, callbacks e framing foram explicitadas de forma conservadora. A revisão final examinou ownership, ponteiros, liberação parcial de lotes, limites de IDs, reinicialização, composição de módulos e consistência entre código e documentação.

docs.text: Communication and the INER protocol ¶ The examples use tcb::span for byte views and zeus::expected for results. See C++17 byte views and results . INER and LightnerX ¶ INER is a semantic protocol. It defines the meaning and organization of messages, but does not define sockets, addressing, threads, or the transmission mechanism. LightnerX implements the protocol's message types and provides networking components based on GameNetworkingSockets. The division is: Responsibility INER LightnerX Meaning of Event, Response, Intention, and Notification Yes Represented by C++ types Message identification Yes MBT::type , correlationId , and status fields Header encoding Yes Packed structures and converters Sockets and connections No Server , Client , and GameNetworkingSockets Execution model No Chosen by the application Roles ¶ Authority ¶ The Authority controls internal states. It receives Intention and Notification from the Obedient and sends Event and Response . In LightnerX, the server typically interprets received messages with: interpreter.obedientInterpret(bytes, registry, connection, connections); Obedient ¶ The Obedient sends intentions to the Authority and receives information about occurrences and results. In LightnerX, the client typically interprets received messages with: interpreter.authorityInterpret(bytes); Message types ¶ Choose the message type according to its purpose and direction. In a typical client-server application, the server acts as the Authority and the client as the Obedient. Message type Direction When to use it Examples Intention Client → Server Request an action that the Authority must evaluate. Move a player, fire a weapon, use an item, join a match. Notification Client → Server Report information without requesting a change to the Authority's internal state. Report measured ping/latency, FPS, or client diagnostics. Event Server → Client Communicate an occurrence or state update from the Authority. A player joined, an entity moved, a projectile spawned, a match started. Response Server → Client Return the outcome of a specific Intention, linked by its correlationId . Movement approved, firing denied because ammunition is insufficient, an action partially applied, or processing failed. These examples describe application-defined messages; LightnerX does not provide built-in gameplay commands or telemetry formats. A Response reports an Intention's outcome, while an Event communicates an occurrence to the relevant clients. Event ¶ Event communicates an occurrence from the Authority. Its header contains: BaseProtocol::size ; MBT::type , used as type_id . The payload, when present, follows the header. Response ¶ Response relates the result to an intention through correlationId and contains a status . The statuses are exposed by constants in the <lightnerx/communication/response.hpp> header: Constant Value Meaning Type used by LightnerX APPROVED_RESPONSE 0 intention fully approved Response DENIED_RESPONSE 1 intention denied UnsuccessfulResponse PARTIALLY_APPROVED_RESPONSE 2 intention partially applied UnsuccessfulResponse FAILURE_RESPONSE 3 internal error during processing Response A failure does not necessarily mean that the intention was denied; the application may decide to try again. UnsuccessfulResponse adds reasonCode to the header of denied or partially approved responses. For partial approval, the meaning of the payload is defined by the application. Intention ¶ Intention requests that the Authority perform an action. Its header contains: BaseProtocol::size ; MBT::type ; correlationId . The intention's payload follows this header. Notification ¶ Notification communicates information to the Authority without requiring state validation, since it does not request a change to the Authority's internal states. Its header contains size and type , followed by the optional payload. On the server, NotificationRegistry specifies which type_id values should be interpreted as Notification : #include <unordered_set> #include <cstdint> #include <lightnerx/communication/notification.hpp> void registerNotifications(lightnerx::communication::NotificationRegistry& registry) { registry.registerId(47); registry.registerIds(std::unordered_set<std::uint16_t>{99, 100}); } The type_id values are defined by the application. There is no universal table of INER types. When receiving messages from the Obedient, registered IDs identify notifications; the others identify intentions. To send notifications, use notification2OutboundMessage . Binary representation ¶ Header structures are packed without additional padding using #pragma pack(push, 1) . The converters copy fields in the machine's native representation; participants must use a compatible representation for these fields and agree on the payload format. Messages from the Authority ¶ The first field uses a combined value: the least significant bit indicates whether the message is a Response , and the remaining fifteen bits represent the size. The table describes the recommended formats for emission: approved, denied and failure responses have no payload; partial approval may carry application-defined bytes. Message Header Recommended content when sending Event 2 bytes of combined size + 2 bytes of type variable payload Response 2 bytes of combined size + 2 bytes of correlationId + 1 byte of status no payload for the statuses represented by Response UnsuccessfulResponse Response structure + 2 bytes of reasonCode variable payload for a partial response When constructing the header, the combined value takes the form: Event: (total_size << 1) | 0 Response: (total_size << 1) | 1 The interpreter retrieves the size with base >> 1 and distinguishes Event from Response with base & 1 . In the headers delivered to the callback, protocol.size already contains the decoded size, without the type bit. Reception currently tolerates additional bytes in responses when the declared total matches the supplied span and the selected header is complete. For approved and failure responses, the interpreter ignores those bytes and delivers an empty payload. For denied and partially approved responses, it delivers all bytes after UnsuccessfulResponse , even though the recommended denied-response format has no payload. protocol.size still includes the complete received message, including any ignored bytes; it can therefore exceed the header size plus the delivered payload size. This reception behavior does not change the recommended emission formats. Converters copy the supplied payload without enforcing status-specific payload rules. Messages from the Obedient ¶ In messages from the Obedient, size directly represents the total message size. Message Header Content Notification 2 bytes of size + 2 bytes of type variable payload Intention 2 bytes of size + 2 bytes of type + 2 bytes of correlationId variable payload The specified size must include the header and payload. Each interpretation call must receive exactly one complete message: the decoded total must equal the supplied span and the header must be complete, otherwise no callback is delivered. Authority messages are limited to 32767 bytes and Obedient messages to 65535 bytes. The interpreter does not split concatenated messages or buffer partial frames. Unknown response statuses are ignored. The converters copy the header and payload into a SteamNetworkingMessage_t ; they do not automatically construct the semantic value of the size field. They throw std::bad_alloc if GNS allocation fails and std::length_error if the allocation size cannot be represented. Identifiers ¶ type_id identifies the semantic type defined by the application and appears in the code as MBT::type . correlationId relates a response to its corresponding intention. The ID received in the server's interpreted message callback is the internal identifier assigned by ConnectionManager . This internal ID belongs to the connection management implementation and is not an INER protocol field. The name originId does not designate a protocol field either. Network destinations use HSteamNetConnection handles, which are distinct from internal IDs and semantic identifiers. Network destinations ¶ lightnerx::network::Target , declared in the <lightnerx/network/target.hpp> header, defines where a queued message will be sent. The static factories create the destination description: Factory Destination Target::single(connection) a specific connection Target::group(connections) all connections in the provided vector Target::broadcast() all connections registered in ConnectionManager Target::broadcast(exceptions) all connections registered in ConnectionManager , except the specified handles Target::group stores the explicit selection of handles. Broadcast queries the ConnectionManager passed to flushAll at flush time, using the mappings maintained by the application. Its exceptions are also HSteamNetConnection handles. Receiving flow ¶ Network -> Server callback -> obedientInterpret -> application callback Network -> Client callback -> authorityInterpret -> application callback MessageInterpreter delivers a lightnerx::communication::Message whose header contains the concrete type in a std::variant and whose payload is a tcb::span<const std::byte> . Callbacks run during the interpretation call. The header is delivered by value, but the span only references the received bytes. In the flow with Server or Client , these bytes are released after the receive callbacks. To retain the payload, copy its bytes during the callback; copying only Message keeps a reference to the same buffer. Sending flow ¶ The usual flow is: Initialize the network and call initMessagesBatcher(capacity) before queuing the first message. Compute the total size of the header and payload. For an Event or Response, encode the first field as (totalSize << 1) | typeBit , with bit 0 for an Event and bit 1 for a Response. For an Intention or Notification, use the total size directly. Create a lightnerx::network::Target . Use the corresponding converter to obtain a lightnerx::network::OutboundMessage . Pass the object to queueMessage(std::move(outbound)) , transferring ownership of the message and destination. Check the queuing result and call flushAll(connectionManager) at the time chosen by the application. Releasing the message becomes the batcher's responsibility, including when queuing returns an error. Example of an Event from the Authority with one byte of payload defined by the application. The function assumes that the network and batcher have been initialized and supports broadcast with or without exceptions: #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" #include <array> #include <cstddef> #include <cstdint> #include <utility> #include <vector> #include <system_error> #include <zeus/expected.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/event.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/message.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/connection_manager.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/message_batch.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/target.hpp> zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> broadcastEvent( const lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager& connections, std::vector<HSteamNetConnection> exceptions = {} ) { const std::array payload{std::byte{0x01}}; const auto totalSize = sizeof(lightnerx::communication::Event) + payload.size(); const lightnerx::communication::Event event{ static_cast<std::uint16_t>(totalSize << 1), 47 }; auto outbound = lightnerx::communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, lightnerx::network::Target::broadcast(std::move(exceptions)) ); const auto queued = lightnerx::network::queueMessage(std::move(outbound)); if (!queued) { return queued; } return lightnerx::network::flushAll(connections); } Call broadcastEvent(connections) for everyone or broadcastEvent(connections, {connectionToSkip}) to exclude a handle, checking the returned zeus::expected . What each step does ¶ queueMessage receives the OutboundMessage from the converter and stores the same message with its destination, without allocating another message or copying the bytes. The call consumes the message: on success, the batcher keeps it until the flush; if the queue is full, it releases it immediately. The caller must not call Release() or reuse the message after passing it to the queue. A null pointer is rejected with invalid_argument . flushAll iterates over pending messages, routes each one according to its destination, and releases the message received from the converter with Release() . All entries are processed and the queue is emptied even when send errors occur. The return value indicates success or the last error encountered among these operations. Batching lets you accumulate multiple messages before a flush. Each entry remains a separate message; payloads are not concatenated. The application decides when to flush, for example at the end of an update. Success indicates that the transport accepted the send operations, without confirming processing by the recipient. For Event and Response , the size field must use the combined value described above. For Intention and Notification , it uses the total size directly. Pending batches can be discarded explicitly with clearMessagesBatcher() and are also released at actual network shutdown. A thrown send exception releases the complete queue before propagating to the caller.

docs.text: Header structures are packed without additional padding using #pragma pack(push, 1) . The converters copy fields in the machine's native representation; participants must use a compatible representation for these fields and agree on the payload format.
docs.title: Binary representation

docs.text: The first field uses a combined value: the least significant bit indicates whether the message is a Response , and the remaining fifteen bits represent the size. The table describes the recommended formats for emission: approved, denied and failure responses have no payload; partial approval may carry application-defined bytes. Message Header Recommended content when sending Event 2 bytes of combined size + 2 bytes of type variable payload Response 2 bytes of combined size + 2 bytes of correlationId + 1 byte of status no payload for the statuses represented by Response UnsuccessfulResponse Response structure + 2 bytes of reasonCode variable payload for a partial response When constructing the header, the combined value takes the form: Event: (total_size << 1) | 0 Response: (total_size << 1) | 1 The interpreter retrieves the size with base >> 1 and distinguishes Event from Response with base & 1 . In the headers delivered to the callback, protocol.size already contains the decoded size, without the type bit. Reception currently tolerates additional bytes in responses when the declared total matches the supplied span and the selected header is complete. For approved and failure responses, the interpreter ignores those bytes and delivers an empty payload. For denied and partially approved responses, it delivers all bytes after UnsuccessfulResponse , even though the recommended denied-response format has no payload. protocol.size still includes the complete received message, including any ignored bytes; it can therefore exceed the header size plus the delivered payload size. This reception behavior does not change the recommended emission formats. Converters copy the supplied payload without enforcing status-specific payload rules.
docs.title: Messages from the Authority

docs.text: In messages from the Obedient, size directly represents the total message size. Message Header Content Notification 2 bytes of size + 2 bytes of type variable payload Intention 2 bytes of size + 2 bytes of type + 2 bytes of correlationId variable payload The specified size must include the header and payload. Each interpretation call must receive exactly one complete message: the decoded total must equal the supplied span and the header must be complete, otherwise no callback is delivered. Authority messages are limited to 32767 bytes and Obedient messages to 65535 bytes. The interpreter does not split concatenated messages or buffer partial frames. Unknown response statuses are ignored. The converters copy the header and payload into a SteamNetworkingMessage_t ; they do not automatically construct the semantic value of the size field. They throw std::bad_alloc if GNS allocation fails and std::length_error if the allocation size cannot be represented.
docs.title: Messages from the Obedient

docs.text: type_id identifies the semantic type defined by the application and appears in the code as MBT::type . correlationId relates a response to its corresponding intention. The ID received in the server's interpreted message callback is the internal identifier assigned by ConnectionManager . This internal ID belongs to the connection management implementation and is not an INER protocol field. The name originId does not designate a protocol field either. Network destinations use HSteamNetConnection handles, which are distinct from internal IDs and semantic identifiers.
docs.title: Identifiers

docs.text: lightnerx::network::Target , declared in the <lightnerx/network/target.hpp> header, defines where a queued message will be sent. The static factories create the destination description: Factory Destination Target::single(connection) a specific connection Target::group(connections) all connections in the provided vector Target::broadcast() all connections registered in ConnectionManager Target::broadcast(exceptions) all connections registered in ConnectionManager , except the specified handles Target::group stores the explicit selection of handles. Broadcast queries the ConnectionManager passed to flushAll at flush time, using the mappings maintained by the application. Its exceptions are also HSteamNetConnection handles.

docs.text: Network -> Server callback -> obedientInterpret -> application callback Network -> Client callback -> authorityInterpret -> application callback MessageInterpreter delivers a lightnerx::communication::Message whose header contains the concrete type in a std::variant and whose payload is a tcb::span<const std::byte> . Callbacks run during the interpretation call. The header is delivered by value, but the span only references the received bytes. In the flow with Server or Client , these bytes are released after the receive callbacks. To retain the payload, copy its bytes during the callback; copying only Message keeps a reference to the same buffer.
docs.title: Receiving flow

docs.text: The usual flow is: Initialize the network and call initMessagesBatcher(capacity) before queuing the first message. Compute the total size of the header and payload. For an Event or Response, encode the first field as (totalSize << 1) | typeBit , with bit 0 for an Event and bit 1 for a Response. For an Intention or Notification, use the total size directly. Create a lightnerx::network::Target . Use the corresponding converter to obtain a lightnerx::network::OutboundMessage . Pass the object to queueMessage(std::move(outbound)) , transferring ownership of the message and destination. Check the queuing result and call flushAll(connectionManager) at the time chosen by the application. Releasing the message becomes the batcher's responsibility, including when queuing returns an error. Example of an Event from the Authority with one byte of payload defined by the application. The function assumes that the network and batcher have been initialized and supports broadcast with or without exceptions: #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" #include <array> #include <cstddef> #include <cstdint> #include <utility> #include <vector> #include <system_error> #include <zeus/expected.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/event.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/message.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/connection_manager.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/message_batch.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/target.hpp> zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> broadcastEvent( const lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager& connections, std::vector<HSteamNetConnection> exceptions = {} ) { const std::array payload{std::byte{0x01}}; const auto totalSize = sizeof(lightnerx::communication::Event) + payload.size(); const lightnerx::communication::Event event{ static_cast<std::uint16_t>(totalSize << 1), 47 }; auto outbound = lightnerx::communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, lightnerx::network::Target::broadcast(std::move(exceptions)) ); const auto queued = lightnerx::network::queueMessage(std::move(outbound)); if (!queued) { return queued; } return lightnerx::network::flushAll(connections); } Call broadcastEvent(connections) for everyone or broadcastEvent(connections, {connectionToSkip}) to exclude a handle, checking the returned zeus::expected .
docs.title: Sending flow

docs.text: queueMessage receives the OutboundMessage from the converter and stores the same message with its destination, without allocating another message or copying the bytes. The call consumes the message: on success, the batcher keeps it until the flush; if the queue is full, it releases it immediately. The caller must not call Release() or reuse the message after passing it to the queue. A null pointer is rejected with invalid_argument . flushAll iterates over pending messages, routes each one according to its destination, and releases the message received from the converter with Release() . All entries are processed and the queue is emptied even when send errors occur. The return value indicates success or the last error encountered among these operations. Batching lets you accumulate multiple messages before a flush. Each entry remains a separate message; payloads are not concatenated. The application decides when to flush, for example at the end of an update. Success indicates that the transport accepted the send operations, without confirming processing by the recipient. For Event and Response , the size field must use the combined value described above. For Intention and Notification , it uses the total size directly. Pending batches can be discarded explicitly with clearMessagesBatcher() and are also released at actual network shutdown. A thrown send exception releases the complete queue before propagating to the caller.

docs.text: C++17 byte views and results ¶ Byte views with span ¶ Include <tcb/span.hpp> for tcb::span . A span refers to contiguous elements owned elsewhere. Copying the view leaves ownership with the original buffer. Receive callback views expire after dispatch. Copy the bytes during the callback if you need to retain them. Construct the view from a contiguous container, an array, or a pointer and count. For a slice previously built from container iterators, pass a pointer and the element count. Use std::size_t{0} for a zero count to disambiguate the pointer-and-count constructor from the pointer-pair constructor. The backport has no .at() member, so check a dynamic index against size() before accessing it. The CMake target propagates one contract policy across translation units. A contract violation terminates the program in both Debug and Release. Use first , last and subspan to select a slice, and tcb::as_bytes to view its object representation. #include <array> #include <cassert> #include <cstddef> #include <tcb/span.hpp> int main() { std::array<int, 3> values{10, 20, 30}; tcb::span<int, 3> all{values}; const tcb::span<const int> empty{values.data(), std::size_t{0}}; assert(empty.empty()); auto tail = all.subspan<1>(); static_assert(decltype(tail)::extent == 2); tail[0] = 25; assert(values[1] == 25); const auto bytes = tcb::as_bytes(all); assert(bytes.size() == values.size() * sizeof(int)); } For the complete interface and bounds-checking options, see tcbrindle/span . First steps ¶ The examples use tcb::span for byte views and zeus::expected for results. See C++17 byte views and results . This guide shows the essential flow for setting up a server and a client. The examples use LightnerX components directly and leave the execution model to the application. Each program is built as a separate application. Server ¶ The server receives bytes from clients, forwards those bytes to MessageInterpreter , and receives interpreted messages through a callback. #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" #include <cstddef> #include <cstdint> #include <iostream> #include <type_traits> #include <variant> #include <tcb/span.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/intention.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/message.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/notification.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/connection_manager.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/server.hpp> int main() { lightnerx::network::Server server; lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager connections{10, 10}; lightnerx::communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; lightnerx::communication::NotificationRegistry registry; registry.registerId(47); server.addClientConnectedCallback( [&connections, &server](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (!connections.add(connection)) { const auto disconnected = server.disconnectConnection(connection, false); if (!disconnected) { std::cout << "Failed to disconnect: " << disconnected.error().message() << '
'; } } } ); server.addClientDisconnectedCallback( [&connections](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (const auto id = connections.getClientId(connection)) { connections.remove(*id); } } ); server.addClientReceivedMessageCallback( [&interpreter, &registry, &connections]( tcb::span<const std::byte> bytes, HSteamNetConnection connection ) { interpreter.obedientInterpret( bytes, registry, connection, connections ); } ); interpreter.addObedientInterpretedMessageCallback( [](lightnerx::communication::Message message, std::uint16_t clientId) { std::cout << "Message received from client " << clientId << '
'; std::visit([](const auto& header) { using Header = std::remove_cv_t<std::remove_reference_t<decltype(header)>>; if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Intention>) { std::cout << "Intention " << header.mbt.type << ", correlation " << header.correlationId << '
'; } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Notification>) { std::cout << "Notification " << header.mbt.type << '
'; } }, message.header); } ); const auto started = server.start(45333, 2500); if (!started) { std::cout << "Failed to start: " << started.error().message() << '
'; return 1; } while (true) { if (const auto updated = server.update(); !updated) { std::cout << "Update failed: " << updated.error().message() << '
'; break; } } server.close(); return 1; } The connection callback must update the ConnectionManager , because the interpreter uses this object to map the connection to the ID delivered to the interpreted message callback. The lambdas capture the components by reference to connect them. Keep these objects alive as long as their callbacks may run. The received payload points to the network message's bytes; copy the bytes during the callback if you need to use them later. Client ¶ The client forwards bytes received from the server to the authorityInterpret method. #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" #include <cstddef> #include <iostream> #include <type_traits> #include <variant> #include <tcb/span.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/event.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/message.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/response.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/client.hpp> int main() { lightnerx::network::Client client; lightnerx::communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; client.addServerReceivedMessageCallback( [&interpreter](tcb::span<const std::byte> bytes) { interpreter.authorityInterpret(bytes); } ); interpreter.addAuthorityInterpretedMessageCallback( [](lightnerx::communication::Message message) { std::visit([](const auto& header) { using Header = std::remove_cv_t<std::remove_reference_t<decltype(header)>>; if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Event>) { std::cout << "Event " << header.mbt.type << '
'; } else if constexpr ( std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Response> || std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::UnsuccessfulResponse> ) { std::cout << "Response to intention " << header.correlationId << ": status " << static_cast<unsigned>(header.status) << '
'; if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::UnsuccessfulResponse>) { std::cout << "Reason " << header.reasonCode << '
'; } } }, message.header); } ); if (const auto started = client.start(); !started) { std::cout << "Failed to start: " << started.error().message() << '
'; return 1; } if (const auto connected = client.connect("127.0.0.1", 45333); !connected) { std::cout << "Failed to connect: " << connected.error().message() << '
'; return 1; } while (true) { if (const auto updated = client.update(1); !updated) { std::cout << "Update failed: " << updated.error().message() << '
'; break; } } return 1; } connect() initiates the connection, and update() processes network callbacks and available messages. isConnected() can be used to query the state observed by the client. Execution model ¶ The server.update() and client.update() methods are called by the application. They can run on the main thread, on a dedicated thread, or within the consuming project's existing execution loop. The application chooses the number of threads and the interval between updates. Run these server and client examples in separate processes so each wrapper can own its LightnerX runtime. Keep wrappers at a fixed address for their lifetime. Receive callbacks run during update() , and interpretation callbacks run on the thread that calls the interpreter. When sharing components across threads, handle synchronization in the application. For the batcher, serialize initialization, queuing, clearing and flush calls, which operate on the same queue. Callback exceptions propagate after resource cleanup; catch them around update() if the application intends to continue. See callback behavior for supported reentrant operations. Batch sending ¶ With the network initialized by Server::start() , Client::start() , or lightnerx::network::networkInit() , reserve space in the batcher before queuing the first message. Include <lightnerx/network/message_batch.hpp> and call: lightnerx::network::initMessagesBatcher(64); The destination is defined by lightnerx::network::Target . The following function creates an Event , routes it to a group, and sends the queue. It assumes the initialization above and returns the result of queuing or flushing to the caller. The same flow applies to the other message converters. #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" #include <cstddef> #include <cstdint> #include <utility> #include <vector> #include <system_error> #include <tcb/span.hpp> #include <zeus/expected.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/event.hpp> #include <lightnerx/communication/message.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/connection_manager.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/message_batch.hpp> #include <lightnerx/network/target.hpp> zeus::expected<void, std::error_code> sendEventToGroup( tcb::span<const std::byte> payload, std::vector<HSteamNetConnection> receivers, const lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager& connections ) { const auto totalSize = sizeof(lightnerx::communication::Event) + payload.size(); if (totalSize > 0x7fff) { return zeus::unexpected(std::make_error_code(std::errc::message_size)); } const lightnerx::communication::Event event{ static_cast<std::uint16_t>(totalSize << 1), 47 }; auto outbound = lightnerx::communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, lightnerx::network::Target::group(std::move(receivers)) ); const auto queued = lightnerx::network::queueMessage(std::move(outbound)); if (!queued) { return queued; } return lightnerx::network::flushAll(connections); } queueMessage receives the OutboundMessage created by the converter and takes ownership of the message and its destination, without reallocating the message or copying its bytes. If the queue is full, the call releases the message immediately and returns an error. If queuing is accepted, flushAll releases the message after the send attempt. Pass an existing object with std::move(outbound) or pass the converter's result directly to queueMessage . After the call, do not access, release, or requeue the consumed message, including in the event of an error. Since message is a raw pointer, std::move does not automatically set it to null in the original object. The header and payload provided to the converter remain owned by the application. With handles obtained by the client or through the server's connection callbacks, the available destinations are: auto oneClient = lightnerx::network::Target::single(connection); auto selectedClients = lightnerx::network::Target::group({firstConnection, secondConnection}); auto everyone = lightnerx::network::Target::broadcast(); auto everyoneElse = lightnerx::network::Target::broadcast({connectionToSkip}); These calls only describe destinations. You can queue several messages and run flushAll(connections) at the end of an application step; the immediate flush shown in the function is a choice made for the example. Next steps ¶ See Communication and the INER protocol to understand headers, destinations, and sending flows. See API reference for networking components, messages, Target , and the batcher.

The dependency's public interfaces and build requirements were checked without changing its source. The network layer owns GNS initialization, client/server lifecycle, connection IDs, routing and a shared outbound queue.
